Controlling this boundary layer to a minimal thickness suppresses interface brittleness and ensures superior coating adhesion during mechanical processing.

# Microstructural Engineering and Optimization of Advanced Aluminum-Zinc Protective Coatings

## Abstract
Continuous hot-dip aluminum-zinc (Al-Zn) coatings are widely utilized to protect steel substrates against environmental corrosion by combining the sacrificial protection of zinc with the passive barrier properties of aluminum. However, standard formulations often suffer from poor formability and accelerated localized degradation due to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases and uncontrolled pure zinc microconstituents. This paper presents an optimized coating formulation engineered through precise quaternary elemental ratios (Al-Zn-Mg-Si) and strictly controlled solidification thermodynamics. By regulating the phase fractions—specifically prioritizing primary solid-solution aluminum ($\alpha$-Al) and fine eutectoid Al-Zn phases while constraining brittle intermetallics and pure zinc regions—this engineered coating achieves exceptional mechanical ductility, interfacial adhesion, and long-term corrosion resistance.

---

## 1. Introduction and Background
Metallic coatings are the primary line of defense against atmospheric and chemical corrosion for structural steel. Traditional hot-dip galvanized (pure Zn) and conventional 55% Al-Zn (Galvalume-type) coatings offer substantial protection; however, modern industrial applications require materials that undergo aggressive mechanical forming without microcracking or delamination. 

The primary failure mode in conventional Al-Zn coatings stems from uncontrolled phase transformations during solidification. As the liquid coating cools, iron from the steel substrate diffuses into the liquid metal, forming thick, extremely brittle Fe-Al and Fe-Al-Si intermetallic compounds (IMCs) at the interface. Simultaneously, coarse, pure zinc-rich phases can segregate within the coating matrix, creating localized pathways for rapid galvanic consumption and structural embrittlement. 

To overcome these structural limitations, an advanced quaternary alloy system composed of aluminum, zinc, magnesium, and silicon has been engineered. By microalloying and precisely controlling solidification kinetics, the resulting microstructure minimizes brittle phases and optimizes the volumetric distribution of highly durable primary and eutectoid phases.

---

## 2. Chemical Composition and Microalloying Strategy
The chemistry of the optimized coating bath relies on a carefully balanced quaternary ratio designed to suppress undesirable phase transformations while maximizing passive barrier efficiency:

*   **Aluminum (Al):** Serves as the structural matrix, forming a dense, self-healing oxide ($Al_2O_3$) surface layer that provides high-temperature resistance and long-term passive barrier protection.
*   **Zinc (Zn):** Provides sacrificial cathodic protection to the underlying steel substrate at cut edges and scratch sites.
*   **Magnesium (Mg):** Microalloyed to alter corrosion product morphology. Mg promotes the formation of stable, insoluble corrosion products such as Simonkolleite and hydrotalcite-like phases, significantly lowering the corrosion rate of zinc-rich areas.
*   **Silicon (Si):** Added primarily to control interfacial diffusion kinetics. Silicon reduces the solubility and activity of iron in the molten bath, effectively retarding the overgrowth of brittle Fe-Al intermetallic layers during hot-dipping.

---

## 3. Microstructural Architecture and Microphase Thresholds
The performance of the optimized coating relies on achieving precise volumetric and cross-sectional phase constraints. Through tailored cooling protocols post-dipping, the solidifying microstructure is forced into targeted equilibrium and non-equilibrium transformations, yielding a highly specific microstructural architecture across its cross-sectional area:

```
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                   Passive Oxide Surface Layer                    |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                                                  |
|   Coating Matrix (≥ 50% Primary α-Al + Fine Eutectoid Al-Zn)    |
|                                                                  |
|   [ Restricted Pure Zn Phase: ≤ 25% ]                            |
|   [ Distributed Intermetallic Phase: ≤ 9% ]                      |
|                                                                  |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|   Interfacial Intermetallic Layer (Fe-Al-Si): ≤ 2 μm             |
+==================================================================+
|                        Steel Substrate                           |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### 3.1 Primary $\alpha$-Al and Eutectoid Phases ($\ge 50\%$)
The structural backbone of the coating consists of primary solid-solution aluminum ($\alpha$-Al) dendrites combined with a fine, dispersed eutectoid aluminum-zinc phase. Together, these constituents must comprise **at least 50% of the cross-sectional area**. The continuous network of $\alpha$-Al provides structural ductility and acts as a mechanical buffer, while the fine eutectoid distribution ensures uniform, micro-galvanic protection without localized matrix collapse.

### 3.2 Restriction of Pure Zinc Phase ($\le 25\%$)
Coarse, free pure zinc phases tend to corrode preferentially at high rates, leaving behind porous channels that undermine coating integrity. In this engineered formulation, the pure zinc phase is strictly constrained to **25% or less of the cross-sectional area**. By forcing excess zinc into refined eutectoid structures or solid solutions with aluminum and magnesium, rapid sacrificial depletion is significantly attenuated.

### 3.3 Matrix Intermetallic Phase Control ($\le 9\%$)
Intermetallic compound (IMC) phases within the coating matrix (such as binary $Mg_2Zn$ or complex ternary phases) can increase hardness but severely impair ductility if over-concentrated. The overall concentration of intermetallic phases throughout the internal matrix is strictly limited to **9% or less of the cross-sectional area**, preventing internal stress concentrations and microcrack propagation under mechanical strain.

### 3.4 Interfacial Intermetallic Layer Thickness ($\le 2\ \mu\text{m}$)
The bond interface between the steel substrate and the alloy coating is typically susceptible to the growth of hard, brittle $Fe_2Al_5$ and $Fe_Al_3$ intermetallic layers. In this optimized system, Si addition and rapid thermal quenching restrict the thickness of this interfacial intermetallic layer to **2 $\mu$m or less**. Keeping this brittle layer extremely thin prevents delamination and flaking during severe deformation processes, such as deep drawing or roll forming.

---

## 4. Performance Metrics and Structural Integrity
By controlling the composition and phase fractions within these precise boundary conditions, the engineered Al-Zn coating demonstrates superior performance over conventional protective coatings:

1.  **Enhanced Formability:** By limiting the intermetallic layer thickness to $\le 2\ \mu\text{m}$ and controlling internal brittle phases to $\le 9\%$, the coating exhibits high bendability. It can accommodate tight radii bending ($T$-bend tests) without microcracking at the interface.
2.  **Synergistic Corrosion Resistance:** The combined presence of Mg and Si within a matrix dominant in primary aluminum and fine eutectoid phases ($\ge 50\%$) yields a complex passivating film upon exposure to atmospheric corrosive agents. Salt spray tests demonstrate significantly delayed initiation of red rust compared to traditional galvanized coatings of equivalent thickness.
3.  **Mechanical Integrity:** The reduced fraction of unalloyed, soft pure zinc ($\le 25\%$) improves wear and scratch resistance, ensuring structural protection remains intact during transport, installation, and operational service.

---

## 5. Conclusion
The optimization of aluminum-zinc protective coatings requires a deliberate shift from simple elemental balancing to precise microstructural engineering. By restricting brittle intermetallic compounds ($\le 9\%$ matrix, $\le 2\ \mu\text{m}$ interface) and unalloyed zinc phases ($\le 25\%$), while promoting ductile primary aluminum and refined eutectoid Al-Zn microconstituents ($\ge 50\%$), this advanced chemical formulation successfully reconciles the trade-off between corrosion protection and mechanical formability. The resulting material provides superior structural integrity and long-term durability for high-performance industrial applications.

It is the most omnipresent word in the English language, yet it glides across our lips virtually unnoticed. Three simple letters—T, H, E—forming a single, unaccented syllable. It carries no imagery of its own. You cannot draw it, you cannot taste it, and if left standing alone on a blank page, it feels entirely hollow. 

Yet, "the" is perhaps the most powerful linguistic tool we possess. It is the master of specificity, the architect of focus, and the bridge between the infinite and the immediate.

To understand the quiet majesty of "the," one only needs to contrast it with its cousin, the indefinite article "a." To speak of *a* day is to acknowledge the endless, rhythmic passage of time—one blip among billions. But to speak of *the* day is to summon memory, destiny, or catastrophe. *A* choice is merely an option; *the* choice is a crossroad. *A* lover is a fleeting presence; *the* lover is a life transformed. By changing a single letter, "the" collapses a universe of possibilities into a single, concrete reality. 

There is a distinct gravity to this tiny word. It bestows authority and majesty upon whatever noun it chooses to accompany. A vast body of water is impressive, but *The* Ocean becomes an ancient, living entity. A collection of stars is a galaxy, but *The* Universe encompasses all that ever was and ever will be. It is no coincidence that we attach it to our most absolute concepts: *The* Truth, *The* Past, *The* Future, and, ultimately, *The* End. 

In the architecture of thought, "the" acts as an anchor for human consciousness. Without it, our language would be a chaotic drift of vague categories and detached concepts. "The" points a definitive finger. It commands us: *Look here. Pay attention to this exact thing, right now.* It plucks a single object out of the ambient noise of existence and shines a spotlight upon it.

We spend our lives searching for "the"—the right job, the perfect moment, the one person who understands us. We strive to move from being *a* face in the crowd to *the* person who made a difference. 

Unassuming and quiet, "the" works tirelessly in the background of our thoughts. It reminds us that amidst an infinite sea of "a's" and "an's," we are living in *this* world, in *this* body, sharing *the* singular, fragile present.

# SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

### [Technical Problem]
An object of the present invention is to provide an Al-Zn-Si-Mg plated steel sheet having superior flat-surface corrosion resistance, cut-edge corrosion resistance, and bend formability by precisely controlling the fractional areas, distribution, and scale of specific microstructural phases within the plating layer and at the substrate interface.

Another object of the present invention is to prevent premature coating delamination and micro-cracking during severe mechanical deformation by optimizing the thickness of the interfacial intermetallic layer.

---

### [Technical Solution]
According to an aspect of the present invention, there is provided an Al-Zn-Si-Mg plated steel sheet comprising:
* a steel substrate;
* an intermetallic layer (30) formed on at least one surface of the steel substrate; and
* an Al-Zn-Si-Mg plating layer formed on the intermetallic layer (30).

In one embodiment, the chemical composition of the plating layer comprises:
* **Al:** 40.0 mass% to 65.0 mass%
* **Si:** 0.5 mass% to 3.0 mass%
* **Mg:** 1.0 mass% to 5.0 mass%
* with the balance being **Zn** and incidental impurities.

The cross-sectional microstructure of the Al-Zn-Si-Mg plating layer comprises:
1. **First Structure (11):** A primary α-Al dendrite phase present in an area fraction of **45 area% to 70 area%** relative to the total cross-sectional area of the plating layer.
2. **Eutectoid Structure (14):** A fine lamellar Al-Zn eutectoid transformation structure present in an area fraction of **10 area% to 30 area%** relative to the total cross-sectional area of the plating layer, wherein the average lamellar spacing within the eutectoid structure (14) is in the range of **30 nm to 200 nm**.
3. **Zn Phases (15):** Interdendritic Zn-rich phases (including fine Mg-containing intermetallic precipitates dispersed therein) present in an area fraction of **5 area% to 20 area%** relative to the total cross-sectional area of the plating layer, wherein the Zn phases (15) have an average grain size (equivalent circle diameter) of **0.2 µm to 3.0 µm**.

The **intermetallic layer (30)** formed at the interface between the steel substrate and the plating layer comprises an Fe-Al-Si-Zn alloy phase and has an average thickness of **0.2 µm to 2.5 µm** (preferably **0.5 µm to 1.5 µm**).

Preferably, the total combined area fraction of the first structure (11), the eutectoid structure (14), and the Zn phases (15) constitutes at least **85 area%** of the total cross-sectional area of the plating layer.

---

### [Advantageous Effects]
According to the present invention, by controlling the area fraction of the **first structure (11)** to 45–70 area%, the primary barrier corrosion resistance and structural integrity of the coating layer are secured. 

By maintaining the **eutectoid structure (14)** within 10–30 area% with a fine lamellar spacing of 30–200 nm, and restricting the **Zn phases (15)** to 5–20 area% with an average size of 0.2–3.0 µm, the sacrificial anode mechanism is optimized. This significantly improves cut-edge corrosion resistance while suppressing excessive local galvanic corrosion.

Furthermore, by controlling the thickness of the **intermetallic layer (30)** within the range of 0.2 µm to 2.5 µm, cracking at the interface during press forming or bending is effectively suppressed, providing exceptional plating adhesion and workability.

# PATENT SPECIFICATION DISCLOSURE

## TITLE OF THE INVENTION
**CORROSION-RESISTANT Al-Zn-Si COATED STEEL SHEET HAVING OPTIMIZED MICROSTRUCTURAL PHASE FRACTIONS AND CONTROLLED INTERLAYER THICKNESS**

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF PREFERRED EMBODIMENTS

### 1. Chemical Composition of the Coating Layer
The hot-dip metallic coating layer formed on a surface of a steel substrate comprises, in weight percent (wt%):
*   **Aluminum (Al):** 45.0% to 65.0%
*   **Silicon (Si):** 1.0% to 3.0%
*   **Magnesium (Mg):** 0.5% to 3.0% (optional)
*   **Iron (Fe):** 0.1% to 3.0% (unavoidable impurity from the substrate bath dissolution)
*   **Balance:** Zinc (Zn) and unavoidable impurities.

*Mechanism:* Aluminum provides long-term barrier corrosion resistance through oxidation passivation, while Zinc provides sacrificial galvanic protection at sheared edges. Silicon suppresses the excessive growth of an brittle Fe-Al intermetallic phase during hot-dipping.

---

### 2. Microstructural Configuration and Phase Area Fractions

The microstructure of the coating layer cross-section consists of a primary dendrite matrix, an interdendritic eutectic mixture, and an interfacial intermetallic layer situated directly adjacent to the steel substrate. 

When measured on a polished cross-section perpendicular to the substrate interface using Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) backscattered electron (BSE) imaging combined with Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) image analysis over an evaluation area of at least $10,000\,\mu\text{m}^2$:

1.  **$\alpha$-Al Primary Solid Solution Phase (Al-rich phase):**
    *   **Phase Characteristics:** Face-centered cubic (FCC) structure containing dissolved Zn (up to 15 wt%) and trace Si. It forms primary dendrites during solidification.
    *   **Area Fraction:** **50.0% to 75.0%** relative to the total cross-sectional area of the coating layer (excluding the interfacial IMC layer).
    *   **Preferred Range:** 55.0% to 68.0%.

2.  **$\eta$-Zn Solid Solution Phase (Zn-rich phase):**
    *   **Phase Characteristics:** Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure present predominantly within the interdendritic regions. Contains dissolved Al (less than 1.0 wt%).
    *   **Area Fraction:** **20.0% to 42.0%** relative to the total cross-sectional area of the coating layer.
    *   **Preferred Range:** 25.0% to 38.0%.

3.  **Elemental Silicon / Si-rich Phase:**
    *   **Phase Characteristics:** Precipitated primary Si particles or fine eutectic Si phase within the interdendritic channels.
    *   **Area Fraction:** **0.8% to 3.5%** relative to the total cross-sectional area of the coating layer.

---

### 3. Interfacial Intermetallic Compound (IMC) Layer

To ensure optimal coating adhesion during severe plastic deformation (e.g., press forming, deep drawing) and to prevent flaking or micro-cracking, the growth of the reaction layer between the iron (Fe) in the steel substrate and the Al-Zn-Si coating alloy is strictly controlled.

*   **Layer Composition:** The IMC layer predominantly comprises ternary or quaternary alloy phases selected from the group consisting of $\tau_5$-$\text{Fe}_2\text{Al}_7\text{Si}$, $\theta$-$\text{Fe}_4\text{Al}_{13}$, $\eta$-$\text{Fe}_2\text{Al}_5$, and complex $\text{Fe-Al-Zn-Si}$ phases.
*   **Average Thickness ($d_{\text{avg}}$):** Controlled within the range of **0.2 $\mu$m to 1.5 $\mu$m**.
*   **Maximum Thickness ($d_{\text{max}}$):** The maximum peak thickness of the IMC layer across any continuous $100\,\mu\text{m}$ interface segment shall **not exceed 2.0 $\mu$m** (preferably **$\le 1.2\,\mu\text{m}$**).

---

## REPRESENTATIVE PATENT CLAIMS

**1. A metallic coated steel sheet comprising:**
a steel substrate; and 
a metallic coating layer formed on at least one surface of the steel substrate, 
**wherein** the metallic coating layer has a chemical composition comprising:
*   45.0 to 65.0 wt% Al;
*   1.0 to 3.0 wt% Si; and
*   a balance of Zn and unavoidable impurities,

**characterized in that** the cross-sectional microstructure of the metallic coating layer comprises:
*   an **$\alpha$-Al solid solution phase** present at an area fraction of **50.0% to 75.0%**;
*   an **$\eta$-Zn solid solution phase** present at an area fraction of **20.0% to 42.0%**; and
*   an **intermetallic compound (IMC) layer** disposed at the interface between the steel substrate and the metallic coating layer, wherein the **maximum thickness of the IMC layer is 2.0 $\mu$m or less**.

**2. The metallic coated steel sheet according to claim 1,** 
wherein the area fraction of the $\alpha$-Al solid solution phase is **55.0% to 68.0%**, and the area fraction of the $\eta$-Zn solid solution phase is **25.0% to 38.0%**.

**3. The metallic coated steel sheet according to claim 1 or 2,** 
wherein the average thickness ($d_{\text{avg}}$) of the IMC layer is in the range of **0.3 $\mu$m to 1.2 $\mu$m**.

**4. The metallic coated steel sheet according to any one of claims 1 to 3,** 
wherein the IMC layer comprises a binary or ternary Fe-Al-Si crystalline phase selected from $\tau_5$-$\text{Fe}_2\text{Al}_7\text{Si}$, $\theta$-$\text{Fe}_4\text{Al}_{13}$, and combinations thereof.

**5. The metallic coated steel sheet according to any one of claims 1 to 4,** 
wherein the metallic coating layer further comprises **0.5 wt% to 3.0 wt% Mg**.

**6. The metallic coated steel sheet according to claim 5,** 
wherein the microstructure further comprises a binary or ternary eutectic phase containing $\text{MgZn}_2$ Laves phase or $\text{Mg}_2\text{Si}$ phase dispersed within the interdendritic regions.

Below is an example of a typical English translation of a patent specification paragraph (derived from standard Patent English styling used by WIPO, USPTO, and EPO) describing a hot-dip Al-Zn coated steel sheet.

***

### Example Patent Paragraph (English Translation)

> **[0035]**  
> A hot-dip Al-Zn alloy-coated steel sheet according to one aspect of the present invention comprises a base steel sheet and a hot-dip Al-Zn alloy coating layer formed on at least one surface of the base steel sheet. The chemical composition of the chemical coating layer comprises, in terms of mass%, **Al: 45.0% to 70.0%**, **Si: 1.0% to 3.0%**, **Mg: 0.5% to 5.0%**, and **Cr: 0.01% to 0.50%**, with the balance being **Zn and unavoidable impurities**. Furthermore, the chemical composition of the base steel sheet comprises, in terms of mass%, **C: 0.02% to 0.15%**, **Si: 0.01% to 0.50%**, **Mn: 0.20% to 2.00%**, **P: 0.030% or less**, and **S: 0.010% or less**, with the remainder being **Fe and impurities**. 
>
> **[0036]**  
> In a cross-sectional microstructure of the coating layer observed along the thickness direction, the coating layer comprises an **intermetallic compound layer** formed at the interface with the base steel sheet, and a **main coating layer** formed on the intermetallic compound layer. The intermetallic compound layer has an **average thickness of 0.5 µm to 3.0 µm** and contains an Al-Fe-Si-Zn quaternary alloy phase. In the main coating layer, an **α-Al primary phase** and an **Al-Zn-Mg ternary eutectic structure** are present, wherein the **area fraction of the α-Al primary phase is 50% to 75%** relative to the total cross-sectional area of the main coating layer, and the **mean secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) of the α-Al primary phase is 1.2 µm to 4.5 µm**. The average particle size of Mg-containing intermetallic compounds precipitated in the eutectic structure is **0.1 µm to 1.0 µm**. Note that these microstructural metrics are calculated by polishing a cross-section along the thickness direction, taking a backscattered electron image (BSE) using a Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) at 2000× magnification over a field of view of 100 µm × 50 µm, and performing quantitative image analysis on at least five arbitrary fields of view.

***

### Key Patent Terminology & Translation Notes

If you are translating similar metallurgical patents (often from Japanese or Chinese source texts), keep these standard conventions in mind:

| Source Term Context | Standard Patent English Translation | Notes / Variations |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 質量% / 重量% | **mass%** or **wt%** | "mass%" is standard for EPO/WIPO; "wt%" is common in USPTO. |
| 残部 / 余量 | **with the balance being...** / ** remainder being...** | Standard transition for chemical composition balance. |
| 断面金属組織 / 截面金相组织 | **cross-sectional microstructure** | Refers to the structure observed along the sheet's thickness cut. |
| 膜厚 / 厚度 | **thickness** / **average thickness** | Often specified as "mean thickness" or "average thickness". |
| 界面合金層 | **intermetallic compound layer** | Also referred to as "interfacial alloy layer". |
| デンドライトアーム間隔 | **dendrite arm spacing (DAS)** | Usually specified as "secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS)". |
| 面積率 / 面积百分比 | **area fraction** | Used for quantifying phase proportions in 2D microscopy. |
| 不可避的不純物 | **unavoidable impurities** | Legalese standard in steel/metallurgy patents. |

# METALLURGICAL SPECIFICATION: ZINC-ALUMINUM-SILICON (Zn-Al-Si) CORROSION-RESISTANT COATING LAYER

**Specification Number:** SPEC-MS-ZAS-004  
**Classification:** Hot-Dip / Thermal Surface Coating, Corrosion Resistant  
**System:** High-Performance Zn-Al-Si Ternary Alloy System  

---

## 1. SCOPE

1.1 **General:** This specification covers the technical, metallurgical, microstructural, and quality acceptance requirements for a hot-dip continuous/batch or thermally processed Zinc-Aluminum-Silicon (Zn-Al-Si) corrosion-resistant metallic coating applied to ferrous substrates (carbon steel, low-alloy steel).

1.2 **Application:** Designed for extreme atmospheric, marine, and industrial corrosive environments requiring combined cathodic protection (sacrificial Zn action) and passive barrier protection (Al-rich passive film and Si-modified interface).

---

## 2. CHEMICAL COMPOSITION

The chemical composition of the final solidified coating layer shall conform to the limits specified in **Table 1**, as determined by Glow Discharge Optical Emission Spectrometry (GD-OES), Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectroscopy (ICP-OES), or Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS).

### Table 1: Chemical Composition Limits (Weight Percent)
| Element | Minimum (wt%) | Maximum (wt%) | Nominal Target (wt%) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Aluminum (Al)** | 10.00 | 40.00 | 25.00 |
| **Silicon (Si)** | 0.05 | 4.00 | 1.50 |
| **Iron (Fe)** *(Interdiffusion/Dissolution)* | — | 1.50 | 0.50 |
| **Lead (Pb)** | — | 0.010 | < 0.003 |
| **Cadmium (Cd)** | — | 0.005 | < 0.002 |
| **Tin (Sn)** | — | 0.020 | < 0.005 |
| **Zinc (Zn)** | Balance | Balance | Balance (~73.0) |

---

## 3. MICROSTRUCTURAL CONSTITUENTS & AREA FRACTIONS

The solidified microstructure shall consist of primary aluminum-rich dendrites, a fine binary/ternary zinc-aluminum eutectic matrix, dispersed primary/secondary silicon-rich phases, and an ultrathin steel-coating interfacial intermetallic layer.

Microstructural evaluation shall be performed on cross-sectional metallographic mounts prepared according to **ASTM E3** and evaluated using SEM-BSE (Backscattered Electron) image analysis per **ASTM E1245** / **ASTM E562**.

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Top Surface (Passive Oxide Layer)                                 |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
|                                                                   |
|   (  \  Primary α-Al Dendrites (Al-rich core)                     |
|   \   ) Area Fraction: 15.0 - 48.0%                               |
|                                                                   |
|   ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~   |
|   Interdendritic Zn-Al Eutectic Matrix (η-Zn + α-Al lamellae)      |
|   Area Fraction: 48.0 - 82.0%                                     |
|                                                                   |
|   [▲] [▲] Dispersed Elemental Silicon (Si) Particles/Needles      |
|   Area Fraction: 0.1 - 4.5%                                       |
|                                                                   |
|===================================================================|
| Fe-Al-Si Intermetallic Interfacial Layer (Thickness ≤ 2.5 µm)     |
|===================================================================|
| Ferrous Substrate (Steel Base)                                    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### 3.1 Microstructural Area Fraction Ranges
The relative area fractions of constituent phases measured across a representative cross-section (excluding the substrate) shall meet the limits in **Table 2**.

#### Table 2: Microstructural Constituent Area Fractions
| Microstructural Constituent | Area Fraction Range (% Area)* | Nominal Target @ 25% Al, 1.5% Si (% Area) | Morphological Characteristics |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary $\alpha$-Al Phase** *(Al-rich solid solution)* | **15.0% – 48.0%** | **32.0% ± 3.0%** | Equiaxed or cellular dendrites; supersaturated with Zn; grain size 2–15 $\mu m$. |
| **Binary/Ternary Eutectic Matrix** *($\eta$-Zn + $\alpha$-Al)* | **48.0% – 82.0%** | **65.0% ± 4.0%** | Fine lamellar or anomalous eutectic structure in interdendritic regions. |
| **Silicon Phase** *(Elemental $\diamondsuit$-Si / Si-rich precipitates)* | **0.1% – 4.5%** | **1.8% ± 0.5%** | Fine acicular needles or modified globular/dendritic particles. |
| **Interfacial Compound Layer** *(Fe-Al-Si intermetallics)* | **0.5% – 3.0%** | **1.2% ± 0.3%** | Continuous, ultra-thin reaction layer at the substrate interface. |
| **Inclusions / Porosity / Defects** | **< 1.0%** | **< 0.2%** | Maximum allowable void fraction or dross contamination. |

*\*Note: Area fraction scales non-linearly with total weight percentages of Al and Si. The primary $\alpha$-Al phase scales directly with Al wt%.*

---

## 4. PHASE MORPHOLOGY AND SPECIFICATIONS

### 4.1 Primary $\alpha$-Aluminum Phase ($\alpha$-Al)
*   **Composition:** Aluminum-rich solid solution ($>70 \text{ wt\% Al}$ within the phase prior to low-temperature spinodal decomposition).
*   **Dendrite Arm Spacing (DAS):** Secondary Dendrite Arm Spacing (SDAS) shall be maintained between **1.0 $\mu m$ and 4.0 $\mu m$** to ensure optimal ductility and corrosion resistance. Fast cooling rates ($\ge 20^\circ\text{C/s}$) during solidification are required to enforce this limit.
*   **Decomposition:** Room temperature spinodal decomposition into sub-micron zinc-rich precipitate clusters ($\eta$-phase) within the primary dendrite cores is acceptable and expected.

### 4.2 Interdendritic Eutectic Matrix
*   **Structure:** Fine, coupled lamellar or script-like mixture of Zinc-rich ($\eta$-Zn, hexagonal close-packed) and Aluminum-rich ($\alpha$-Al, face-centered cubic) phases.
*   **Lamellar Interplanar Spacing:** Must not exceed **0.5 $\mu m$** to prevent localized pit initiation in the eutectic zone.

### 4.3 Silicon Phase ($\diamondsuit$-Si)
*   **Morphology:** Elemental Silicon crystals. Unmodified cooling yields coarse, acicular (needle-like) Si phase which degrades coating formability. 
*   **Modification Requirement:** If Si content exceeds 1.0 wt%, chemical modification (e.g., Sr, Na, or Sb addition at 50–200 ppm) or rapid cooling MUST be employed to spheroidize or refine the Si particles into a globular morphology with an aspect ratio $< 3:1$.
*   **Maximum Particle Size:** No individual Si particle shall exceed **5.0 $\mu m$** in length/major axis.

### 4.4 Interfacial Reaction Layer (Fe-Al-Si)
*   **Composition:** Ternary intermetallic inhibition layer comprising $\tau_5$-$\text{Fe}_2\text{Al}_7\text{Si}$, $\theta$-$\text{Fe}_4\text{Al}_{13}$, and $\eta$-$\text{Fe}_2\text{Al}_5$.
*   **Thickness Control:** The total interfacial layer thickness shall not exceed **2.5 $\mu m$** (target: $0.8 - 1.5 \ \mu m$).
*   **Rationale:** Silicon suppresses the excessive growth of brittle Fe-Al binary intermetallics ($\text{Fe}_2\text{Al}_5$). An interfacial thickness $>2.5 \ \mu m$ will result in coating flaking during secondary forming operations (bending, drawing).

---

## 5. PHYSICAL AND MECHANICAL PROPERTIES

| Property | Requirement | Test Standard |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Total Coating Thickness** | $10 - 50 \ \mu m$ (as specified per order) | ASTM B487 / ISO 2178 |
| **Coating Mass** | $60 - 250 \ \text{g/m}^2$ (total both sides) | ASTM A90 |
| **Microhardness (Coating Matrix)**| $110 - 180 \ \text{HV}_{0.02}$ | ASTM E384 |
| **Adhesion / Formability** | 0T to 2T Bend Test (No flaking at 10x magnification) | ASTM D4145 / ISO 7438 |

---

## 6. CORROSION RESISTANCE REQUIREMENTS

### 6.1 Salt Spray (Fog) Resistance
When subjected to continuous neutral salt spray (NSS) testing in accordance with **ASTM B117 / ISO 9227**:
*   **Red Rust Initiation:** No base metal corrosion (red rust $> 5\%$ of surface area) for a minimum of **2,500 hours** for a $20 \ \mu m$ single-side coating thickness.
*   **White Rust Formation:** Zinc oxidation products (white rust) are permitted, but self-passivation by aluminum-rich oxides ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$) must slow further oxidation within 120 hours of exposure.

### 6.2 Cyclic Corrosion Testing (CCT)
Per **ISO 11997-1 (Cycle A) / SAE J2334**:
*   Must withstand a minimum of **120 cycles** without substrate perforation
